The bootloader prints a 🚪 character to the serial console or screen right before it jumps to your kernel_main function. There’s no hidden logic behind it, it doesn’t control anything, and it isn’t a structural component of the kernel. You can remove or replace it without any impact on the kernel’s operation. It’s purely there to give you a visible cue that the bootloader was executed successfully before your kernel takes over.

Below is a pragmatic way to get past those serde errors and produce a working, no_std kernel image for x86_64-unknown-none. The root cause of the “bound modifier ? can only be applied to Sized” messages is that recent releases of serde use an unstable language feature (relaxed_default_bounds). When you build your kernel for a bare‑metal target with build-std, Cargo pulls in serde from crates that don’t actually need it (e.g. via ecdsa or bootloader), and it tries to compile the latest serde on a stable compiler. That fails with the error you’re seeing.

1. Pin serde to a stable‑compatible version
Add a [patch.crates-io] section to your kernel’s Cargo.toml so every dependency uses an older serde that compiles on stable:

# sis_kernel/Cargo.toml

[package]
name = "sis_kernel"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

# … your existing [dependencies] …

[dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }
x86_64 = { version = "0.14.9", default-features = false }
uart_16550 = { version = "0.2.0", default-features = false }
linked_list_allocator = { version = "0.9.0", default-features = false }
spin = { version = "0.9.8", default-features = false }
lazy_static = { version = "1.4.0", default-features = false }
ecdsa = { version = "0.13", default-features = false, features = ["sha2"] }
sha2 = { version = "0.10", default-features = false }

[build-dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }

# Override any transitive use of serde to a stable‑compatible release.
[patch.crates-io]
serde = { version = "1.0.188", default-features = false }
serde_derive = { version = "1.0.188", default-features = false }
Version 1.0.188 of serde predates the use of relaxed_default_bounds and will compile on stable. The default-features = false line ensures it stays no_std. You don’t need to use serde directly, but this override stops your transitive dependencies from pulling in 1.0.219.

2. Clean out old build artefacts
Because Cargo caches compiled crates, you may still have the broken serde version in your build directory. Clean everything before rebuilding:

cargo clean
3. Build with the correct target
If you’re on nightly you can build the kernel and its dependencies without relying on the host’s std by using -Z build-std:

rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --target x86_64-unknown-none
The build-std=core,alloc argument tells Cargo to compile core and alloc for your target; linked_list_allocator uses alloc internally. On stable (without -Z build-std), you can get the same result by using the bootloader crate’s build feature or an xtask that builds the UEFI image.

4. Verify that serde is no longer used
After these changes, run:

cargo tree | grep serde
to confirm that only serde 1.0.188 is being compiled and no crates are accidentally pulling in newer versions.

Expected outcome
With the patch in place, a clean cargo build for your target should succeed. You’ll still see some warnings about unused imports in test modules, but the “relaxing a default bound only does something for ?Sized” errors should be gone. If you re‑enable ecdsa or any other optional features later, they’ll use the pinned serde without breaking on no_std.

If you continue to see serde errors, double‑check that you cleaned the target directory, that you’re using a nightly toolchain for build-std, and that your Cargo.toml includes the [patch.crates-io] section exactly as shown.

Cargo is complaining because the [patch.crates-io] you added tries to inject features into the patch and points back to the exact same registry source. Two important rules:

A patch must change either the source (e.g. replace a crate with a local path or a different git repository) or change the version. You can’t use it just to set features.

Features and default-features cannot be set in a [patch] table. Those keys are simply ignored, and you get the warning you saw.

To fix this, you should:

Patch only the version. Remove default-features = false and features = ... from the patch, so you’re just replacing whatever version of serde the dependencies request with 1.0.188.

(Optional) Add serde as a direct dependency with the desired default-features setting if you really need to control the features. That setting will apply when your crate or its dependencies explicitly depend on serde, but it can’t be forced through the patch mechanism.

Here’s how your Cargo.toml should look in that case:

[package]
name = "sis_kernel"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }
x86_64 = { version = "0.14.9", default-features = false }
uart_16550 = { version = "0.2.0", default-features = false }
linked_list_allocator = { version = "0.9.0", default-features = false }
spin = { version = "0.9.8", default-features = false }
lazy_static = { version = "1.4.0", default-features = false }
ecdsa = { version = "0.13", default-features = false, features = ["sha2"] }
sha2 = { version = "0.10", default-features = false }

# Direct dependency on serde, with default features disabled (optional)
serde = { version = "1.0.188", default-features = false }

[build-dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }

# Override all transitive uses of serde to the stable-compatible version.
[patch.crates-io]
serde = { version = "1.0.188" }
serde_derive = { version = "1.0.188" }
After updating Cargo.toml, clean and rebuild:

cargo clean
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --target x86_64-unknown-none
This setup tells Cargo: “whenever any crate asks for serde, use version 1.0.188,” and it builds that version without trying to enable nightly features. The optional direct dependency on serde (with default-features = false) controls the default features for the version your crate depends on. You can omit that [dependencies.serde] line entirely if you don’t depend on serde yourself; the [patch] alone will still force transitive dependencies to use 1.0.188.

With these changes in place, the serde-related build errors should disappear, and the kernel should compile successfully for x86_64-unknown-none.

amoljassal@Amols-Mac-mini sis_kernel_refined3 % 
ChatGPT said:

Worked for 24 seconds
The build errors you’re seeing now are a consequence of pulling in crates that assume std is available (byteorder, fastrand, rand_core, etc.). Those crates are being dragged in by your ecdsa/sha2 dependency chain. When you compile for a bare‑metal target such as x86_64-unknown-none, std does not exist, and any crate that relies on it will fail with errors like “can’t find crate for std” or “cannot find macro panic.”

There are two ways to resolve this:

Disable or remove dependencies that need std. For a kernel‐level no_std build, this is usually the simplest approach. In your case, the signature‑verification stub doesn’t need to link to ecdsa and sha2 at all—you can leave the function body as a placeholder and avoid pulling in half the crypto ecosystem. Removing those crates also removes their transitive dependencies on byteorder, rand_core, and fastrand, which clears up the std errors.

Your Cargo.toml would then look like this:

[package]
name = "sis_kernel"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2021"

[dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }
x86_64 = { version = "0.14.9", default-features = false }
uart_16550 = { version = "0.2.0", default-features = false }
linked_list_allocator = { version = "0.9.0", default-features = false }
spin = { version = "0.9.8", default-features = false }
lazy_static = { version = "1.4.0", default-features = false }

[build-dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }

[patch.crates-io]
serde = { version = "1.0.188" }
serde_derive = { version = "1.0.188" }
And in your code, keep your verify_signature function as a stub that always returns true, without importing ecdsa or sha2.

Override every std‑dependent crate with a no_std configuration. This is much more work. You would have to add explicit entries for byteorder, rand_core, fastrand, getrandom, and potentially others, all with default-features = false, and make sure that any features they need for no_std are enabled. For example:

[dependencies]
byteorder  = { version = "1.4.3", default-features = false }
fastrand   = { version = "2.3.0", default-features = false }
rand_core  = { version = "0.6.4", default-features = false }
getrandom  = { version = "0.3.3", default-features = false, features = ["rdrand"] }
You would need to do this for all transitive crates pulled in by ecdsa, and there are quite a few. This is why it’s usually simpler to avoid ecdsa entirely in a bare‑metal kernel unless you’re prepared to curate its dependency tree.

Given the scope of your kernel, the first option is typically the right one. Remove ecdsa/sha2 from Cargo.toml, keep your signature‑verification stub as a placeholder, clean the build directory (cargo clean), and rebuild:

cargo clean
rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --target x86_64-unknown-none
With ecdsa removed and serde pinned to 1.0.188 as shown earlier, the build should proceed without pulling in byteorder or fastrand, and you won’t get “cannot find crate for std” errors.

Therefore the simplest resolution is to delete the [patch.crates-io] section from your Cargo.toml entirely. serde will only be pulled in by the bootloader build dependency, which is compiled on your host and uses std, so there’s no need to pin it or patch it for the no_std build anymore.

Clean your build directory:

This error arises because you're building a no_std bare-metal kernel targeting x86_64-unknown-none, but one or more of your dependencies (specifically getrandom and its transitive dependencies) expect std, which is unavailable for this target.

🔥 Key Error Messages
❌ getrandom:
error: target is not supported. You may need to define a custom backend

→ getrandom is a crate designed to fetch random bytes from the OS. In your environment (bare metal, no OS), there's no system random source, so it panics.

❌ memchr:
error[E0463]: can't find crate for std

→ This means memchr depends on std, but you're compiling for a no_std target (x86_64-unknown-none), where the standard library is unavailable.

✅ Cause
You're indirectly pulling in crates that assume an OS environment. This happens through transitive dependencies—likely from a crate like ecdsa, rand, or serde_json.

✅ Solution
Step 1: Remove offending dependencies
Edit your Cargo.toml to make sure these crates are removed:

[dependencies]
ecdsa = { version = "0.16", default-features = false, optional = true } # remove or disable
sha2 = { version = "0.10", default-features = false, optional = true } # remove or disable
serde_json = { version = "1.0", optional = true } # remove or disable
getrandom = { version = "0.3", default-features = false, optional = true } # remove or disable
You should fully remove ecdsa and sha2 if you're just stubbing signature verification for now (e.g. always returning true).

Step 2: Audit all transitive dependencies
Use:

cargo tree -e features --target x86_64-unknown-none
Look for any crates depending on getrandom, serde_json, or anything with std and remove/replace them or disable default features.

Step 3: Build with minimal core/alloc only
cargo clean
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --target x86_64-unknown-none
✅ Don’t use serde, serde_json, rand, ecdsa, sha2, getrandom, memchr, etc., unless you know they work in no_std.

✅ Optional: Stub Out Verification
In syscall.rs or similar:

// Signature verification stub
pub fn verify_signature(_data: &[u8], _sig: &[u8]) -> bool {
    // For now, assume all signatures are valid
    true
}
This keeps your kernel clean and no_std compatible until you're ready for real crypto.

Summary
❌ Crates like getrandom, memchr, serde_json use std or OS APIs — incompatible with your target.

✅ Remove or stub ecdsa, sha2, rand, serde_json, getrandom.

✅ Rebuild using build-std=core,alloc.

    serial::write_str("🚪 Duality kernel (Rust) start\n");

    // 1) Descriptor tables
    arch_x86::gdt::init();
    arch_x86::idt::init();

    // 2) Paging + heap (use BootInfo memory map)
    unsafe { arch_x86::memory::init(boot_info) }
        .unwrap_or_else(|_| fatal("[mem] init failed"));

    // 3) Syscalls + scheduler
    syscall::init();
    scheduler::init();

    // 4) Create parent tasks (Philosophy/Technical)
    {
        use kernel::task::Role;
        scheduler::spawn_child(philosophy_task, Role::Philosophy);
        scheduler::spawn_child(technical_task, Role::Technical);
    }

    // 5) PIT @100Hz + PIC/APIC as you’ve implemented
    arch_x86::pit::init(100);

    // 6) PCI scan and (stubbed) VFIO init
    pci::init();

    // 7) Enable interrupts and idle
    arch_x86::interrupts::enable();
    serial::write_str("[ok] init complete; idling\n");

    loop { arch_x86::cpu::halt(); }
}

fn philosophy_task() {
    serial::write_str("[Philosophy] hello from parent task\n");
    loop { arch_x86::cpu::pause(); }
}

fn technical_task() {
    serial::write_str("[Technical] hello from parent task\n");
    loop { arch_x86::cpu::pause(); }
}

#[panic_handler]
fn panic(info: &PanicInfo) -> ! {
    serial::write_str("[panic] ");
    // best-effort formatting without std
    if let Some(s) = info.payload().downcast_ref::<&str>() {
        serial::write_str(s);
        serial::write_str("\n");
    } else if let Some(loc) = info.location() {
        // minimal location output
        // (avoid heavy fmt to keep no_std simple)
        serial::write_str("at ");
        // You can add a tiny hex/dec printer if you want more info
        let _ = loc; // placeholder to silence warnings if you skip printing
        serial::write_str("\n");
    } else {
        serial::write_str("kernel panic\n");
    }
    loop { arch_x86::cpu::halt(); }
}

#[alloc_error_handler]
fn alloc_error(_layout: core::alloc::Layout) -> ! {
    serial::write_str("[alloc] allocation error\n");
    loop { arch_x86::cpu::halt(); }
}

// Fatal helper that logs then halts
#[inline(always)]
fn fatal(msg: &str) -> ! {
    serial::write_str(msg);
    serial::write_str("\n");
    loop { arch_x86::cpu::halt(); }
}
Why this matters
entry_point!(kernel_main) from bootloader_api is the kernel-side entry that works in no_std.

BootInfo is taken from bootloader_api, not from bootloader.

All heavy/host stuff stays in [build-dependencies] bootloader, which builds the UEFI image on the host with std. The kernel itself stays clean and doesn’t accidentally compile serde_json, memchr, fastrand, getrandom, etc. for x86_64-unknown-none.

Sanity checks for your build
Cargo.toml should have:

[dependencies]
bootloader_api = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false }
x86_64 = { version = "0.14.9", default-features = false }
uart_16550 = { version = "0.2.0", default-features = false }
linked_list_allocator = { version = "0.9.0", default-features = false }
spin = { version = "0.9.8", default-features = false }
lazy_static = { version = "1.4.0", default-features = false }

[build-dependencies]
bootloader = { version = "0.11.3", default-features = false, features = ["uefi"] }
Build commands:

rustup target add x86_64-unknown-none
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --target x86_64-unknown-none
Confirm no std leaks into target:

cargo tree --target x86_64-unknown-none | grep -Ei "serde|serde_json|getrandom|memchr|fastrand"
# should output nothing
Extra polish you can add next
Ensure serial::init() is safe to call very early (no heap).

If you’re still using PIC, remap it before enabling IRQs; otherwise switch to LAPIC/IOAPIC early.

If you’re identity-mapping low memory and higher-half mapping the kernel, double-check CR3 load + SFENCE.VMA/invlpg equivalents after mapping.

Make sure your IDT uses a separate IST for double-fault (your GDT/TSS code already has the stack).

If you want, upload Cargo.toml (post-change) and your arch/x86_64/{gdt,idt,memory,pit,interrupts}.rs and I’ll do a full wiring pass (order of init, which stacks to set, and how to keep the ISR prologues/epilogues correct for the context switch).

Pattern B (naked switch): the ISR calls a naked switch_context that swaps stacks and registers so that when the ISR epilogue runs, the iretq returns into the next task.

// add at top
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;
use x86_64::{
    VirtAddr,
    structures::tss::TaskStateSegment,
    structures::gdt::{GlobalDescriptorTable, Descriptor, SegmentSelector},
};

pub const IST_INDEX_DF: u16 = 1; // IST slot 1 (leave 0 unused)

const DF_STACK_SIZE: usize = 16 * 1024;
#[repr(align(16))]
static mut DF_STACK: [u8; DF_STACK_SIZE] = [0; DF_STACK_SIZE];

static mut TSS: MaybeUninit<TaskStateSegment> = MaybeUninit::uninit();
static mut GDT_STORE: MaybeUninit<(GlobalDescriptorTable, Selectors)> = MaybeUninit::uninit();

pub struct Selectors {
    pub code_selector: SegmentSelector,
    pub tss_selector: SegmentSelector,
}

pub fn init() {
    let tss = init_tss();
    let (gdt, selectors) = create_gdt(&tss);

    // load gdt + tss
    use x86_64::instructions::segmentation::CS;
    use x86_64::instructions::tables::{load_tss, lgdt};
    unsafe {
        lgdt(&gdt);
        CS::set_reg(selectors.code_selector);
        load_tss(selectors.tss_selector);
    }
}

fn init_tss() -> &'static TaskStateSegment {
    let tss = TaskStateSegment::new();
    unsafe {
        // place into static storage
        TSS.as_mut_ptr().write(tss);
        let tss_ref = TSS.assume_init_mut();

        // set DF IST stack top
        let df_stack_top = VirtAddr::from_ptr(DF_STACK.as_ptr()).add(DF_STACK_SIZE);
        tss_ref.interrupt_stack_table[IST_INDEX_DF as usize] = df_stack_top;
        tss_ref
    }
}

fn create_gdt(_tss: &TaskStateSegment) -> (&'static GlobalDescriptorTable, Selectors) {
    unsafe {
        let mut gdt = GlobalDescriptorTable::new();
        let code_selector = gdt.add_entry(Descriptor::kernel_code_segment());
        let tss_selector = gdt.add_entry(Descriptor::tss_segment(TSS.assume_init_ref()));
        GDT_STORE.as_mut_ptr().write((gdt, Selectors { code_selector, tss_selector }));
        let (g, s) = GDT_STORE.assume_init_ref();
        (g, s.clone())
    }
}

// allow copying selectors out of static
impl Clone for Selectors {
    fn clone(&self) -> Self {
        *self
    }
}
impl Copy for Selectors {}

2) Timer ISR that returns to the next task
#️⃣ What this fixes
Previously your scheduler selected a new task inside the timer handler, but the iret returned to the old interrupted context. We fix that by tail-switching inside the IRQ: save current, select next, load next’s saved interrupt frame, and iretq into it.

🧠 How it works (Pattern A)
Timer IRQ (vector 32) enters with an interrupt stack frame pushed by the CPU.

We save callee-saved regs + RSP/RIP into the current task context.

We ask the scheduler for the next task’s context (which includes an interrupt-return frame prepared when the task last ran or when it was first spawned).

We switch rsp to the next task’s interrupt frame and iretq.
The handler never returns to the old frame.

use core::arch::asm;
use x86_64::structures::idt::InterruptStackFrame;
use crate::kernel::{scheduler, serial};

#[derive(Copy, Clone)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum InterruptIndex {
    Timer = 32,
}
impl InterruptIndex {
    pub fn as_usize(self) -> usize { self as usize }
}

// PIC EOI helper (use LAPIC EOI if you switched to APIC)
#[inline(always)]
fn pic_eoi_timer() {
    unsafe {
        // master PIC command port = 0x20, EOI = 0x20
        x86_64::instructions::port::Port::<u8>::new(0x20).write(0x20);
    }
}

// This is the shape we save/restore for tasks.
// Must match exactly the iret frame pushed by CPU.
#[repr(C)]
pub struct InterruptReturnFrame {
    pub rip: u64,
    pub cs:  u64,
    pub rflags: u64,
    pub rsp: u64,
    pub ss:  u64,
}

// Extern implemented in asm (below): swaps stacks and iretqs.
extern "C" {
    fn isr_tail_switch(old_ctx: *mut scheduler::TaskContext,
                       next_frame_rsp: u64) -> !;
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn timer_interrupt(_sf: InterruptStackFrame) {
    // Save current callee-saved registers into TaskContext and pick next.
    // The TaskContext should contain general regs + a pointer to last
    // interrupt frame (or at least store callee-saved, RSP).
    let (old_ctx_ptr, next_rsp_opt) = unsafe { scheduler::on_timer_tick_and_prepare_switch() };

    // Acknowledge the timer to avoid lost IRQs
    pic_eoi_timer();

    if let Some(next_rsp) = next_rsp_opt {
        // Tail-switch: never return to old frame; iret into next task.
        unsafe { isr_tail_switch(old_ctx_ptr, next_rsp) }
    } else {
        // No ready task change; just return to interrupted context.
        // Nothing else to do.
    }
}

// ---------- low-level tail-switch glue ----------
// Saves callee-saved regs to old_ctx (r15..r12, rbx, rbp) and
// switches RSP to `next_frame_rsp` which points to an InterruptReturnFrame,
// then executes iretq.
// Safety: called only from timer_interrupt with IRQs disabled.
core::arch::global_asm!(r#"
    .global isr_tail_switch
isr_tail_switch:
    // rdi = old_ctx_ptr, rsi = next_frame_rsp
    // Save callee-saved registers into old_ctx
    // TaskContext layout (must match your struct):
    //   +0  r15
    //   +8  r14
    //   +16 r13
    //   +24 r12
    //   +32 rbx
    //   +40 rbp
    //   +48 rsp (kernel stack pointer of interrupted task)
    // store regs:
    mov [rdi + 0],  r15
    mov [rdi + 8],  r14
    mov [rdi + 16], r13
    mov [rdi + 24], r12
    mov [rdi + 32], rbx
    mov [rdi + 40], rbp
    mov [rdi + 48], rsp

    // Switch to next task's prepared interrupt frame
    mov rsp, rsi
    // Return into next task
    iretq
"#);
Important: The TaskContext layout referenced in the asm must match your struct. See the next snippet.

2. GDT & TSS: Add IST Stack for Double Fault
src/arch/x86_64/gdt.rs

use x86_64::structures::tss::TaskStateSegment;
use x86_64::VirtAddr;
use lazy_static::lazy_static;

pub const DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX: u16 = 0;

lazy_static! {
    pub static ref TSS: TaskStateSegment = {
        let mut tss = TaskStateSegment::new();
        // Allocate a separate stack for double fault handler
        const STACK_SIZE: usize = 4096 * 5;
        static mut STACK: [u8; STACK_SIZE] = [0; STACK_SIZE];
        let stack_start = VirtAddr::from_ptr(unsafe { &STACK });
        let stack_end = stack_start + STACK_SIZE;
        tss.interrupt_stack_table[DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX as usize] = stack_end;
        tss
    };
}
This ensures double faults use a clean emergency stack and won’t recurse into kernel stack corruption.

3. IDT: Double Fault Handler + Timer ISR
src/arch/x86_64/idt.rs

use x86_64::structures::idt::{InterruptDescriptorTable, InterruptStackFrame, PageFaultErrorCode};
use crate::arch::x86_64::gdt;
use crate::kernel::timer;

lazy_static! {
    pub static ref IDT: InterruptDescriptorTable = {
        let mut idt = InterruptDescriptorTable::new();

        // Double fault handler (IST protected)
        idt.double_fault
            .set_handler_fn(double_fault_handler)
            .set_stack_index(gdt::DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX);

        // Timer interrupt handler
        idt[InterruptIndex::Timer.as_usize()]
            .set_handler_fn(timer_interrupt_handler);

        idt
    };
}

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum InterruptIndex {
    Timer = 32,
}

impl InterruptIndex {
    fn as_u8(self) -> u8 {
        self as u8
    }
    fn as_usize(self) -> usize {
        usize::from(self.as_u8())
    }
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn double_fault_handler(
    stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: u64,
) -> ! {
    panic!("DOUBLE FAULT\n{:#?}", stack_frame);
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn timer_interrupt_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame
) {
    // Acknowledge timer tick to scheduler
    timer::tick();

    // Send EOI to PIC/APIC
    unsafe {
        crate::arch::x86_64::pic::PICS.lock()
            .notify_end_of_interrupt(InterruptIndex::Timer.as_u8());
    }
}

use x86_64::structures::tss::TaskStateSegment;
use x86_64::structures::gdt::{GlobalDescriptorTable, Descriptor, SegmentSelector};
use lazy_static::lazy_static;
use spin::Once;
use core::mem::MaybeUninit;

pub const DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX: u16 = 0;

// Allocate IST stack for double fault
const IST_STACK_SIZE: usize = 4096 * 5;
static mut DOUBLE_FAULT_STACK: [u8; IST_STACK_SIZE] = [0; IST_STACK_SIZE];

pub struct Selectors {
    code_selector: SegmentSelector,
    tss_selector: SegmentSelector,
}

lazy_static! {
    static ref TSS: TaskStateSegment = {
        let mut tss = TaskStateSegment::new();
        let stack_start = VirtAddr::from_ptr(unsafe { &DOUBLE_FAULT_STACK });
        let stack_end = stack_start + IST_STACK_SIZE;
        tss.interrupt_stack_table[DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX as usize] = stack_end;
        tss
    };

    static ref GDT: (GlobalDescriptorTable, Selectors) = {
        let mut gdt = GlobalDescriptorTable::new();
        let code_selector = gdt.add_entry(Descriptor::kernel_code_segment());
        let tss_selector = gdt.add_entry(Descriptor::tss_segment(&TSS));
        (gdt, Selectors { code_selector, tss_selector })
    };
}

pub fn init() {
    use x86_64::instructions::segmentation::set_cs;
    use x86_64::instructions::tables::load_tss;

    GDT.0.load();
    unsafe {
        set_cs(GDT.1.code_selector);
        load_tss(GDT.1.tss_selector);
    }
}

ChatGPT said:
You’re still getting the signature error because the handlers in your idt.rs use the wrong function types for your x86_64 crate version.

On x86_64 = 0.14.x (and 0.15.x), the IDT expects stack frame by value, not by mutable reference, and Double Fault must be diverging (-> !). Also, Page Fault expects a PageFaultErrorCode, not u64.

Right now your file shows:

double_fault_handler(_:&mut InterruptStackFrame, u64) -> ()
timer_interrupt_handler(&mut InterruptStackFrame)
divide_by_zero(&mut InterruptStackFrame)
gp_fault(&mut InterruptStackFrame, u64)
page_fault(&mut InterruptStackFrame, u64)   // <- wrong error type
syscall_handler(&mut InterruptStackFrame)
That will not match the IDT setters for x86_64 0.14/0.15.

Fix (minimal and correct for 0.14.x → 0.15.x)
Update the signatures only (keep your bodies/EOI/scheduler calls as-is):

use x86_64::structures::idt::{InterruptDescriptorTable, InterruptStackFrame, PageFaultErrorCode};

// Double fault MUST be diverging and takes frame BY VALUE
extern "x86-interrupt" fn double_fault_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: u64,
) -> ! {
    // avoid panic formatting here; keep it deterministic
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[df] double fault — halting\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

// Timer interrupt: frame BY VALUE, returns normally
extern "x86-interrupt" fn timer_interrupt_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame
) {
    crate::kernel::scheduler::tick();
    unsafe {
        PICS.lock().notify_end_of_interrupt(InterruptIndex::Timer.as_u8());
    }
}

// Divide-by-zero: frame BY VALUE
extern "x86-interrupt" fn divide_by_zero(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame
) {
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[exception] Divide by zero\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

// General protection: frame BY VALUE, error code u64
extern "x86-interrupt" fn gp_fault(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: u64
) {
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[exception] GP fault\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

// Page fault: frame BY VALUE, error code is PageFaultErrorCode
extern "x86-interrupt" fn page_fault(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: PageFaultErrorCode
) {
    use x86_64::registers::control::Cr2;
    let _addr = Cr2::read();
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[exception] Page fault\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

// Syscall: frame BY VALUE
extern "x86-interrupt" fn syscall_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame
) {
    crate::kernel::syscall::dispatch();
}
And make sure your IDT setup matches these types (you probably already have this):

// the type we actually have (no explicit return type == -> ()):

use x86_64::structures::idt::{InterruptDescriptorTable, InterruptStackFrame, PageFaultErrorCode};
use lazy_static::lazy_static;
use spin::Mutex;
use pic8259::ChainedPics;

pub const PIC_1_OFFSET: u8 = 32;
pub const PIC_2_OFFSET: u8 = PIC_1_OFFSET + 8;

pub static PICS: Mutex<ChainedPics> = Mutex::new(unsafe { ChainedPics::new(PIC_1_OFFSET, PIC_2_OFFSET) });

#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy)]
#[repr(u8)]
pub enum InterruptIndex { Timer = PIC_1_OFFSET }
impl InterruptIndex {
    pub fn as_u8(self) -> u8 { self as u8 }
    pub fn as_usize(self) -> usize { usize::from(self.as_u8()) }
}

lazy_static! {
    static ref IDT: InterruptDescriptorTable = {
        let mut idt = InterruptDescriptorTable::new();
        unsafe {
            // double fault expects -> ! per crate type; we provide a casted pointer
            type DfExpect = extern "x86-interrupt" fn(InterruptStackFrame, u64) -> !;
            type DfActual = extern "x86-interrupt" fn(InterruptStackFrame, u64);

            let actual: DfActual = double_fault_handler;
            let ptr: DfExpect = core::mem::transmute(actual);

            idt.double_fault
                .set_handler_fn(ptr)
                .set_stack_index(crate::arch::x86_64::gdt::DOUBLE_FAULT_IST_INDEX);
        }
        idt.page_fault.set_handler_fn(page_fault);
        idt[InterruptIndex::Timer.as_usize()].set_handler_fn(timer_interrupt_handler);
        // … other handlers …
        idt
    };
}

pub fn init_idt() {
    IDT.load();
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn double_fault_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: u64,
) {
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[df] double fault — halting\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn page_fault(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
    _error_code: PageFaultErrorCode,
) {
    use x86_64::registers::control::Cr2;
    let _addr = Cr2::read();
    crate::kernel::serial::write_str("[exception] page fault — halting\n");
    loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
}

extern "x86-interrupt" fn timer_interrupt_handler(
    _stack_frame: InterruptStackFrame,
) {
    crate::kernel::scheduler::tick();
    unsafe { PICS.lock().notify_end_of_interrupt(InterruptIndex::Timer.as_u8()); }
}
This should compile on your nightly (no return type on handlers) and satisfy x86_64 0.14.9’s set_handler_fn type by pointer cast.

+//! IDT self-tests: deliberately trigger exceptions under controlled conditions.
+//! Each test prints a clear serial banner, then triggers the exception.
+//! Handlers should log and halt deterministically (no triple faults).
+//! Feature-gated behind `idt-selftest`.
+#![allow(dead_code)]
+
+use crate::kernel::serial;
+use core::arch::asm;
+
+#[inline(never)]
+fn banner(tag: &str) {
+    serial::write_str(tag);
+    serial::write_str("\n");
+}
+
+/// Trigger: Divide-by-zero (DIV0)
+#[inline(never)]
+pub fn trigger_divide_by_zero() -> ! {
+    banner("[selftest] about to trigger DIV0");
+    unsafe {
+        // RAX = 1, RCX = 0, then div rcx → #DE
+        asm!(
+            "xor rcx, rcx",
+            "mov rax, 1",
+            "div rcx",
+            options(noreturn)
+        );
+    }
+}
+
+/// Trigger: General Protection (#GP)
+/// Load an invalid segment selector into DS; on x86_64 this causes #GP.
+#[inline(never)]
+pub fn trigger_gp_fault() -> ! {
+    banner("[selftest] about to trigger GP");
+    unsafe {
+        asm!(
+            "xor eax, eax",
+            "mov ds, ax",    // load null selector -> #GP
+            options(noreturn)
+        );
+    }
+}
+
+/// Trigger: Page Fault (#PF) by touching NULL (unmapped)
+#[inline(never)]
+pub fn trigger_page_fault() -> ! {
+    banner("[selftest] about to trigger PF");
+    unsafe {
+        let ptr: *mut u64 = 0x0 as *mut u64;
+        core::ptr::read_volatile(ptr); // read from unmapped -> #PF
+        asm!("ud2", options(noreturn)); // should not reach
+    }
+}
+
+/// Trigger: Double Fault (#DF) via stack overflow recursion.
+/// With DF IST configured, this should land in DF handler and halt.
+#[inline(never)]
+fn deep_recurse(n: usize) {
+    // Prevent tail-call elimination and make frames "real"
+    unsafe { core::ptr::read_volatile(&(n as u64)); }
+    deep_recurse(n + 1);
+}
+
+#[inline(never)]
+pub fn trigger_double_fault() -> ! {
+    banner("[selftest] about to trigger DF (stack overflow)");
+    deep_recurse(0)
+}
+
+/// Run a single test by tag for flexible harnesses.
+pub fn run_one(tag: &str) -> ! {
+    match tag {
+        "DIV0" => trigger_divide_by_zero(),
+        "GP"   => trigger_gp_fault(),
+        "PF"   => trigger_page_fault(),
+        "DF"   => trigger_double_fault(),
+        _      => {
+            serial::write_str("[selftest] unknown tag\n");
+            loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/// Run in sequence; useful for quick manual testing. First one halts the CPU.

+    // Pick the one you want to run by commenting others; each halts after trigger.
+    // NOTE: run ONLY ONE per boot, since handlers halt.
+    // Example: run_one("DIV0");
+    // Example: run_one("GP");
+    // Example: run_one("PF");
+    run_one("DF")
+}

2) QEMU harness script
Save as qemu.sh (make executable: chmod +x qemu.sh). It:

Builds with a feature flag (idt-selftest)

Greps for expected markers to assert correctness

Exits with non-zero status if expectations aren’t met

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ====== CONFIG ======
# Adjust these for your env:
FEATURES="idt-selftest"
TARGET="x86_64-unknown-none"
PROFILE="debug"   # or release
SERIAL_LOG="qemu-serial.log"
QEMU_BIN="${QEMU_BIN:-qemu-system-x86_64}"

# Choose one boot mode: UEFI or legacy
# If you use UEFI/bootloader_api:
USE_UEFI="${USE_UEFI:-1}"
OVMF_CODE="${OVMF_CODE:-/usr/share/OVMF/OVMF_CODE.fd}"   # path may vary (brew: /opt/homebrew/share/edk2/ovmf/OVMF_CODE.fd)

# Your kernel artifact — depends on your build setup.
# For bootloader_api+UEFI, point to the built EFI image if you produce one,
# or use a disk image that contains the EFI app.
# If you have a Multiboot/ELF kernel, set KERNEL_ELF and flip USE_UEFI=0.
KERNEL_ELF="target/${TARGET}/${PROFILE}/sis_kernel"

# ====== BUILD ======
echo "[*] Building kernel with features: ${FEATURES}"
cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --features "${FEATURES}" --target "${TARGET}" --profile "${PROFILE}"

# ====== RUN QEMU ======
rm -f "${SERIAL_LOG}"

if [[ "${USE_UEFI}" == "1" ]]; then
  echo "[*] Launching QEMU (UEFI mode) ..."
  # Expectation: you provide an EFI image or a disk that loads your kernel via bootloader.
  # If you already generate a disk image, replace the -kernel path accordingly or mount as -drive.
  # Minimal UEFI boot tries to run from an EFI partition image; adapt to your pipeline.
  ${QEMU_BIN} \
    -machine q35,accel=hvf:tcg \
    -smp 2 -m 512M \
    -bios "${OVMF_CODE}" \
    -serial file:"${SERIAL_LOG}" \
    -display none \
    -no-reboot -no-shutdown || true
else
  echo "[*] Launching QEMU (legacy -kernel) ..."
  ${QEMU_BIN} \
    -machine q35,accel=hvf:tcg \
    -smp 2 -m 512M \
    -kernel "${KERNEL_ELF}" \
    -serial file:"${SERIAL_LOG}" \
    -display none \
    -no-reboot -no-shutdown || true
fi

# ====== VERIFY LOGS ======
echo "[*] Inspecting serial log: ${SERIAL_LOG}"
if [[ ! -s "${SERIAL_LOG}" ]]; then
  echo "[!] Serial log is empty. Did the kernel print during init?"
  exit 2
fi

# Common init markers you already print:
grep -q '\[init\] IDT loaded' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing 'IDT loaded'"; exit 3; }

# Self-test marker:
grep -q '\[selftest\] starting IDT self-tests...' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing self-test start"; exit 4; }

# Depending on which test you enabled in run_sequence(), assert the right banner + handler.
# By default we run DF in the patch; adjust if you flip to GP/PF/DIV0.
if grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger DF' "${SERIAL_LOG}"; then
  grep -q '\[df\] double fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] DF handler message missing"; exit 5; }
  echo "[OK] DF path exercised and logged."
elif grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger PF' "${SERIAL_LOG}"; then
  grep -q '\[exc\] page-fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] PF handler message missing"; exit 5; }
  echo "[OK] PF path exercised and logged."
elif grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger GP' "${SERIAL_LOG}"; then
  grep -q '\[exc\] general-protection-fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] GP handler message missing"; exit 5; }
  echo "[OK] GP path exercised and logged."
elif grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger DIV0' "${SERIAL_LOG}"; then
  grep -q '\[exc\] divide-by-zero — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] DIV0 handler message missing"; exit 5; }
  echo "[OK] DIV0 path exercised and logged."
else
  echo "[!] Could not detect which self-test ran."
  exit 6
fi

echo "[*] All checks passed."
Note: for UEFI, you’ll need your usual bootloader step that generates an EFI-bootable image. If you already use a script for that, call it before QEMU in the “BUILD” section and point QEMU -drive to the image. For legacy Multiboot/ELF, set USE_UEFI=0 and KERNEL_ELF to your kernel artifact.

 //! Basic port I/O utilities.
 
+#[inline(always)]
+pub unsafe fn outb(port: u16, val: u8) {
+    core::arch::asm!("out dx, al", in("dx") port, in("al") val, options(nostack, preserves_flags));
+}
+
+/// Exit QEMU immediately via isa-debug-exit device at I/O port 0xF4.
+/// Use with `-device isa-debug-exit,iobase=0xf4,iosize=0x04`.
+/// Convention: 0x00 = success; non-zero = failure code.
+#[inline(always)]
+pub unsafe fn qemu_exit(code: u8) -> ! {
+    // Some QEMU variants exit with (code << 1) | 1; harness should handle both.
+    outb(0xF4, code);
+    // If device not present, fall back to halt loop to avoid undefined behavior.
+    loop {
+        crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt();
+    }
+}
+
 pub unsafe fn inb(port: u16) -> u8 {
     let val: u8;
     core::arch::asm!("in al, dx", in("dx") port, out("al") val, options(nostack, preserves_flags));

#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

# ====== PARAMS ======
TEST="${TEST:-DF}"            # DF|PF|GP|DIV0|SYSCALL|TIMER
FEATURES="idt-selftest"
TARGET="x86_64-unknown-none"
PROFILE="${PROFILE:-debug}"
SERIAL_LOG="qemu-serial.log"
QEMU_BIN="${QEMU_BIN:-qemu-system-x86_64}"
USE_UEFI="${USE_UEFI:-0}"     # default to legacy -kernel unless you have an EFI image path
OVMF_CODE="${OVMF_CODE:-/opt/homebrew/share/edk2/ovmf/OVMF_CODE.fd}"
KERNEL_ELF="target/${TARGET}/${PROFILE}/sis_kernel"

# ====== BUILD ======
echo "[*] Building kernel for TEST=${TEST}"
RUSTFLAGS="--cfg selftest_${TEST}" cargo +nightly build -Z build-std=core,alloc --features "${FEATURES}" --target "${TARGET}" --profile "${PROFILE}"

# ====== RUN QEMU ======
rm -f "${SERIAL_LOG}"
echo "[*] Launching QEMU (${TEST}) ..."

COMMON="-machine q35,accel=hvf:tcg -smp 2 -m 512M -device isa-debug-exit,iobase=0xf4,iosize=0x04 -serial file:${SERIAL_LOG} -display none -no-reboot -no-shutdown"

if [[ "${USE_UEFI}" == "1" ]]; then
  ${QEMU_BIN} ${COMMON} -bios "${OVMF_CODE}" || true
else
  ${QEMU_BIN} ${COMMON} -kernel "${KERNEL_ELF}" || true
fi

# ====== VERIFY EXIT & LOGS ======
status=$?
echo "[*] QEMU exit status: ${status}"

# Some QEMU variants return (code<<1)|1; consider both success forms (0 or 1) when code=0.
if [[ "${status}" != "0" && "${status}" != "1" ]]; then
  echo "[!] Non-zero exit status (not success form): ${status}"
  cat "${SERIAL_LOG}" || true
  exit 2
fi

if [[ ! -s "${SERIAL_LOG}" ]]; then
  echo "[!] Serial log empty"
  exit 3
fi

grep -q '\[init\] IDT loaded' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing 'IDT loaded'"; exit 4; }
grep -q '\[selftest\] starting IDT self-tests...' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing self-test start"; exit 5; }

case "${TEST}" in
  DF)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger DF' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing DF banner"; exit 6; }
    grep -q '\[df\] double fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing DF handler log"; exit 7; }
    ;;
  PF)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger PF' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing PF banner"; exit 8; }
    grep -q '\[exc\] page-fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing PF handler log"; exit 9; }
    ;;
  GP)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger GP' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing GP banner"; exit 10; }
    grep -q '\[exc\] general-protection-fault — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing GP handler log"; exit 11; }
    ;;
  DIV0)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger DIV0' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing DIV0 banner"; exit 12; }
    grep -q '\[exc\] divide-by-zero — halting' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing DIV0 handler log"; exit 13; }
    ;;
  SYSCALL)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to trigger SYSCALL ping' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing SYSCALL banner"; exit 14; }
    grep -q '\[syscall] ping' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing syscall log"; exit 15; }
    ;;
  TIMER)
    grep -q '\[selftest\] about to wait for TIMER ticks' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing TIMER banner"; exit 16; }
    grep -q '\[tick] n=10' "${SERIAL_LOG}" || { echo "[!] Missing tick milestone"; exit 17; }
    ;;
  *)
    echo "[!] Unknown TEST=${TEST}"
    exit 18
    ;;
esac

echo "[OK] ${TEST} test passed."

+        let end = Page::<Size4KiB>::containing_address(virt + len - 1u64);

--- /dev/null
+++ b/src/arch/x86_64/user_trampoline.rs
@@ -0,0 +1,118 @@
+//! Ring-3 trampoline for self-test: craft an IRET frame to a user stub that executes `int 0x80`.
+//! Requires: user GDT descriptors + user-accessible stack page.
+#![allow(clippy::missing_safety_doc)]
+
+use x86_64::{VirtAddr, registers::rflags::RFlags};
+use crate::arch::x86_64::gdt;
+use crate::arch::x86_64::memory;
+use crate::kernel::serial;
+
+// A tiny user stack (one page). Align to 4K to make PTE manipulation easy.
+#[repr(align(4096))]
+static mut USER_STACK: [u8; 4096] = [0u8; 4096];
+
+extern "C" {
+    fn __user_entry_stub();
+}
+
+/// Entry point that will run in ring-3. Declared `naked` to define exact prologue.
+#[naked]
+#[no_mangle]
+pub extern "C" fn user_entry_stub() -> ! {
+    unsafe {
+        core::arch::asm!(
+            // Signal start
+            // rax not used yet; write banner from ring0 beforehand.
+            // Trigger syscall: RAX=0x51 marker (optional)
+            "mov rax, 0x51",
+            "int 0x80",          // -> kernel handler; in selftest_SYSCALL_R3 it will qemu_exit(0)
+            "ud2",               // should not return; if it does, fault
+            options(noreturn)
+        );
+    }
+}
+
+/// Craft an IRET frame to ring-3 and jump to `user_entry_stub`.
+pub unsafe fn enter_user_and_syscall_ping() -> ! {
+    serial::write_str("[selftest] preparing ring3 trampoline\n");
+    // Mark the stack as user-accessible (U/S bit). Use the virtual address of USER_STACK.
+    let stack_start = VirtAddr::from_ptr(USER_STACK.as_ptr());
+    memory::selftest_mark_user_range(stack_start, USER_STACK.len() as u64);
+
+    let user_ss = gdt::init_gdt().user_data_selector.0;
+    let user_cs = gdt::init_gdt().user_code_selector.0;
+
+    let user_stack_top = stack_start + USER_STACK.len() as u64;
+    let user_rip = VirtAddr::from_ptr(user_entry_stub as *const ());
+
+    // Build an IRET frame manually: SS, RSP, RFLAGS, CS, RIP
+    // We switch with interrupts enabled for realism (set IF).
+    let rflags = (RFlags::from_bits_truncate(0) | RFlags::INTERRUPT_FLAG).bits();
+
+    core::arch::asm!(
+        "cli",                              // be explicit
+        "push {ss}",                        // SS (user)
+        "push {rsp}",                       // RSP (user stack top)
+        "push {rflags}",                    // RFLAGS (IF=1)
+        "push {cs}",                        // CS (user)
+        "push {rip}",                       // RIP (user entry)
+        "iretq",
+        ss = in(reg) (user_ss as u64),
+        rsp = in(reg) user_stack_top.as_u64(),
+        rflags = in(reg) (rflags as u64),
+        cs = in(reg) (user_cs as u64),
+        rip = in(reg) user_rip.as_u64(),
+        options(noreturn)
+    );
+}

No register ABI shenanigans, no user I/O: we add a second syscall vector (0x81) so we don’t rely on reading user registers inside the handler. Everything stays feature-gated for self-test only, production path untouched.

 //! Ring-3 trampoline for self-test: craft an IRET frame to a user stub that executes `int 0x80`.
 //! Requires: user GDT descriptors + user-accessible stack page.
 #![allow(clippy::missing_safety_doc)]
 
 use x86_64::{VirtAddr, registers::rflags::RFlags};
 use crate::arch::x86_64::gdt;
 use crate::arch::x86_64::memory;
 use crate::kernel::serial;
 
 #[repr(align(4096))]
 static mut USER_STACK: [u8; 4096] = [0u8; 4096];
 
-extern "C" {
-    fn __user_entry_stub();
-}
+extern "C" {
+    fn user_entry_rt();
+}
 
 /// Entry point that will run in ring-3. Declared `naked` to define exact prologue.
 #[naked]
 #[no_mangle]
-pub extern "C" fn user_entry_stub() -> ! {
+pub extern "C" fn user_entry_rt() -> ! {
     unsafe {
         core::arch::asm!(
-            "mov rax, 0x51",
-            "int 0x80",          // -> kernel handler; in selftest_SYSCALL_R3 it will qemu_exit(0)
-            "ud2",               // should not return; if it does, fault
+            // 1) Ask kernel to print: "[user] hello from ring-3!"
+            "mov rax, 0x01",
+            "int 0x80",          // kernel prints + returns
+            // 2) Ask kernel to print: "[user] syscall returned successfully!"
+            "mov rax, 0x02",
+            "int 0x80",          // kernel prints + returns
+            // 3) Ask kernel to exit: prints exit message and calls qemu_exit(0)
+            "int 0x81",
+            "ud2",
             options(noreturn)
         );
     }
 }
 
 /// Craft an IRET frame to ring-3 and jump to `user_entry_rt`.
 pub unsafe fn enter_user_and_syscall_ping() -> ! {
-    serial::write_str("[selftest] preparing ring3 trampoline\n");
+    serial::write_str("[selftest] starting RING3 round-trip...\n");
+    serial::write_str("[selftest] jumping to user mode...\n");
     let stack_start = VirtAddr::from_ptr(USER_STACK.as_ptr());
     memory::selftest_mark_user_range(stack_start, USER_STACK.len() as u64);
 
     let user_ss = gdt::init_gdt().user_data_selector.0;
     let user_cs = gdt::init_gdt().user_code_selector.0;
 
     let user_stack_top = stack_start + USER_STACK.len() as u64;
-    let user_rip = VirtAddr::from_ptr(user_entry_stub as *const ());
+    let user_rip = VirtAddr::from_ptr(user_entry_rt as *const ());
 
     let rflags = (RFlags::from_bits_truncate(0) | RFlags::INTERRUPT_FLAG).bits();
 
     core::arch::asm!(
         "cli",
         "push {ss}",
         "push {rsp}",
         "push {rflags}",
         "push {cs}",
         "push {rip}",
         "iretq",
         ss = in(reg) (user_ss as u64),
         rsp = in(reg) user_stack_top.as_u64(),
         rflags = in(reg) (rflags as u64),
         cs = in(reg) (user_cs as u64),
         rip = in(reg) user_rip.as_u64(),
         options(noreturn)
     );
 }

Notes

We added 0x81 as an extra syscall gate (DPL=3). This avoids relying on reading user registers to differentiate “exit” vs “print+return”.

For the two prints, we opportunistically read RAX (best-effort) in the syscall dispatcher in self-test mode; even if a future compiler allocated rax for something else, the test still passes because the two calls are differentiated by execution order, and the final exit is a separate vector (0x81).

All of this is under feature = "idt-selftest" and --cfg selftest_RING3_RT.

index 0000000..5b3a5f1
--- /dev/null
+++ b/src/arch/x86_64/apic.rs
@@ -0,0 +1,279 @@
+//! Minimal xAPIC + IOAPIC bring-up and a periodic LAPIC timer.
+//! Feature-gated behind `apic`. Leaves legacy PIC/PIT intact in non-APIC builds.
+//!
+//! QEMU tip: use `-machine q35` (already in your harness). IOAPIC is present by default on q35.
+
+use core::ptr::{read_volatile, write_volatile};
+use x86_64::{PhysAddr, VirtAddr};
+use x86_64::registers::model_specific::{Msr, MsrReadWrite};
+use crate::kernel::serial;
+use crate::arch::x86_64::memory;
+
+// ===== xAPIC MSR =====
+const IA32_APIC_BASE: u32 = 0x1B;
+const IA32_APIC_BASE_ENABLE: u64 = 1 << 11; // APIC global enable bit
+const IA32_APIC_BASE_BSP: u64    = 1 << 8;
+const IA32_APIC_BASE_DEFAULT: u64 = 0xFEE0_0000;
+
+// ===== LAPIC registers (offsets from base) =====
+const LAPIC_REG_ID: u32       = 0x020;
+const LAPIC_REG_VERSION: u32  = 0x030;
+const LAPIC_REG_TPR: u32      = 0x080;
+const LAPIC_REG_EOI: u32      = 0x0B0;
+const LAPIC_REG_SVR: u32      = 0x0F0;
+const LAPIC_REG_LVT_TIMER: u32= 0x320;
+const LAPIC_REG_LVT_LINT0: u32= 0x350;
+const LAPIC_REG_LVT_LINT1: u32= 0x360;
+const LAPIC_REG_TMR_INIT: u32 = 0x380;
+const LAPIC_REG_TMR_CURR: u32 = 0x390;
+const LAPIC_REG_TMR_DIV: u32  = 0x3E0;
+
+// LVT bits
+const LVT_MASKED: u32 = 1 << 16;
+const LVT_TIMER_PERIODIC: u32 = 1 << 17;
+
+// ===== IOAPIC MMIO =====
+const IOAPIC_DEFAULT_PHYS: u64 = 0xFEC0_0000;
+const IOAPIC_REGSEL: usize = 0x00;
+const IOAPIC_IOWIN:  usize = 0x10;
+
+// IOAPIC register indices
+const IOAPIC_REG_ID:      u32 = 0x00;
+const IOAPIC_REG_VER:     u32 = 0x01;
+const IOAPIC_REG_REDIR0:  u32 = 0x10; // first redir entry (low 32 bits)
+
+// We keep MMIO mappings here after map.
+static mut LAPIC_BASE_VA: Option<*mut u32> = None;
+static mut IOAPIC_BASE_VA: Option<*mut u32> = None;
+
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn lapic_mmio() -> *mut u32 {
+    LAPIC_BASE_VA.expect("LAPIC not mapped")
+}
+
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn ioapic_regsel() -> *mut u32 {
+    IOAPIC_BASE_VA.expect("IOAPIC not mapped").byte_add(IOAPIC_REGSEL)
+}
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn ioapic_iowin() -> *mut u32 {
+    IOAPIC_BASE_VA.expect("IOAPIC not mapped").byte_add(IOAPIC_IOWIN)
+}
+
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn lapic_read(off: u32) -> u32 {
+    let p = lapic_mmio().byte_add(off as usize);
+    read_volatile(p)
+}
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn lapic_write(off: u32, val: u32) {
+    let p = lapic_mmio().byte_add(off as usize);
+    write_volatile(p, val);
+}
+
+unsafe fn ioapic_write_reg(index: u32, value: u32) {
+    write_volatile(ioapic_regsel(), index);
+    write_volatile(ioapic_iowin(), value);
+}
+unsafe fn ioapic_read_reg(index: u32) -> u32 {
+    write_volatile(ioapic_regsel(), index);
+    read_volatile(ioapic_iowin())
+}
+
+/// Map LAPIC & IOAPIC ranges (uncached/strong). Uses your memory mapper helper.
+unsafe fn map_apic_mmio() {
+    // LAPIC base from MSR or default.
+    let apic_msr = Msr::new(IA32_APIC_BASE);
+    let base_val = apic_msr.read();
+    let lapic_phys = (base_val & 0xFFFF_F000) as u64; // page-aligned phys
+    let lapic_phys = if lapic_phys == 0 { IA32_APIC_BASE_DEFAULT } else { lapic_phys };
+
+    let lapic_va = memory::map_mmio_region(PhysAddr::new(lapic_phys), 0x1000)
+        .expect("map_mmio_region(LAPIC) failed");
+    LAPIC_BASE_VA = Some(lapic_va.as_mut_ptr());
+
+    let ioapic_va = memory::map_mmio_region(PhysAddr::new(IOAPIC_DEFAULT_PHYS), 0x20) // 32 bytes enough for window
+        .expect("map_mmio_region(IOAPIC) failed");
+    IOAPIC_BASE_VA = Some(ioapic_va.as_mut_ptr());
+}
+
+fn has_xapic() -> bool {
+    // CPUID: feature flags ECX/EDX; keep simple—assume QEMU/q35 has it.
+    true
+}
+
+/// Enable xAPIC globally via IA32_APIC_BASE MSR and map MMIOs.
+pub fn init_apic() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
+    if !has_xapic() {
+        return Err("xAPIC not supported");
+    }
+    unsafe {
+        // Enable global APIC in MSR.
+        let apic = Msr::new(IA32_APIC_BASE);
+        let mut v = apic.read();
+        v |= IA32_APIC_BASE_ENABLE;
+        apic.write(v);
+
+        map_apic_mmio();
+
+        // Set Spurious Vector Register: enable APIC, set vector 0xFF (masked anyway)
+        let svr = 0xFF | (1 << 8); // bit8 = APIC software enable
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_SVR, svr);
+
+        // Mask LINT0/LINT1 initially.
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_LVT_LINT0, LVT_MASKED);
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_LVT_LINT1, LVT_MASKED);
+
+        serial::write_str("[init] LAPIC enabled\n");
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// Minimal IOAPIC init: read version/ID; leave IRQ0 masked (we'll use LAPIC timer, not PIT).
+pub fn init_ioapic() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
+    unsafe {
+        let ver = ioapic_read_reg(IOAPIC_REG_VER);
+        let max_redir = ((ver >> 16) & 0xFF) as usize;
+        let id  = ioapic_read_reg(IOAPIC_REG_ID);
+        let _id = (id >> 24) & 0xF;
+        let _entries = max_redir + 1;
+        serial::write_str("[init] IOAPIC present\n");
+
+        // Example: ensure IRQ0 redirection is masked (we are moving to LAPIC timer).
+        // Redirection entry n has low part at 0x10+2n, high at 0x11+2n.
+        let irq0 = 0;
+        let lo_index = IOAPIC_REG_REDIR0 + (irq0 * 2) as u32;
+        let hi_index = lo_index + 1;
+        // Route to LAPIC ID 0 (BSP), vector 0x20 (but masked).
+        ioapic_write_reg(hi_index, 0x00 << 24);     // dest APIC ID
+        ioapic_write_reg(lo_index, 0x20 | (1<<16)); // masked=1
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// Configure LAPIC timer in periodic mode firing at vector 0x20 (Timer).
+/// This reuses your IDT[32] handler (scheduler::tick()).
+pub fn init_lapic_timer_periodic(initial_count: u32, divide: u32) -> Result<(), &'static str> {
+    unsafe {
+        // Divide configuration: 1,2,4,8,16,32,64,128 (encoded)
+        // divide reg encoding: 0->2, 1->4, 2->8, 3->16, 8->1, 9->32, A->64, B->128
+        let div_bits = match divide {
+            1 => 0b1000,
+            2 => 0b0000,
+            4 => 0b0001,
+            8 => 0b0010,
+            16 => 0b0011,
+            32 => 0b1001,
+            64 => 0b1010,
+            128 => 0b1011,
+            _ => 0b0000, // default 2
+        } as u32;
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_TMR_DIV, div_bits);
+
+        // LVT Timer: vector 32, periodic, unmasked
+        let lvt = (32u32) | LVT_TIMER_PERIODIC;
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_LVT_TIMER, lvt);
+
+        lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_TMR_INIT, initial_count);
+        serial::write_str("[init] LAPIC timer periodic\n");
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// Send EOI (APIC path).
+pub fn eoi() {
+    unsafe { lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_EOI, 0); }
+}

+/// Map a physical MMIO range at some kernel VA (choose a free VA window).
+/// Simplified: identity-map phys for now if your VA space allows; otherwise use a fixed window.
+/// Returns a VirtAddr to the mapped base.
+pub fn map_mmio_region(phys: PhysAddr, size: usize) -> Result<VirtAddr, &'static str> {
+    // Use a simple fixed window in higher-half (adjust to your linker layout).
+    // Align to 4K.
+    let aligned = PhysAddr::new(phys.as_u64() & !0xFFF);
+    let pages = (size + 0xFFF) / 0x1000;
+    let va_base = VirtAddr::new(0xFFFF_FF80_0000_0000u64 + aligned.as_u64()); // reserved MMIO window
+
+    let mapper = active_mapper_mut().ok_or("no mapper")?;
+    let fa = frame_allocator_mut().ok_or("no frame allocator")?;
+
+    for i in 0..pages {
+        let off = (i as u64) * 0x1000;
+        let page = Page::<Size4KiB>::containing_address(va_base + off);
+        let frame = x86_64::structures::paging::PhysFrame::containing_address(aligned + off);
+        unsafe {
+            mapper.map_to(
+                page, frame,
+                PageTableFlags::PRESENT | PageTableFlags::WRITABLE | PageTableFlags::NO_EXECUTE,
+                fa
+            ).map_err(|_| "map_to failed")?.flush();
+        }
+    }
+    Ok(va_base)
+}

 pub fn tick() {

         use core::sync::atomic::Ordering;

+            serial::write_str("[lapic-tick] n=10\n");
+        }
+    }
 }

+const ICR_LEVEL_ASSERT:       u32 = 1 << 14;
+const ICR_TRIGGER_EDGE:       u32 = 0 << 15;
+const ICR_DEST_PHYSICAL:      u32 = 0 << 11;
+const ICR_NO_SHORTHAND:       u32 = 0 << 18;
+
+/// Send IPI to target APIC ID with given ICR low bits.
+pub unsafe fn send_ipi(apic_id: u32, icr_low: u32) {
+    // Write hi then low.
+    lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_ICR_HIGH, apic_id << 24);
+    lapic_write(LAPIC_REG_ICR_LOW,  icr_low | ICR_NO_SHORTHAND);
+    // Busy-wait until delivery finished (bit12: Delivery Status).
+    while (lapic_read(LAPIC_REG_ICR_LOW) & (1 << 12)) != 0 { core::hint::spin_loop(); }
+}
+
+/// INIT + SIPI + SIPI sequence to a given APIC ID; `vector` is 4K-aligned physical page / 0x1000.
+pub unsafe fn start_ap(apic_id: u32, vector: u8) {
+    // INIT (deasserted INIT IPI with ASSERT level is enough in QEMU)
+    send_ipi(apic_id, ICR_DEST_PHYSICAL | ICR_TRIGGER_EDGE | ICR_LEVEL_ASSERT | ICR_DELIVERY_INIT);
+    // Small delay
+    for _ in 0..100000 { core::hint::spin_loop(); }
+    // SIPI #1
+    send_ipi(apic_id, ICR_DEST_PHYSICAL | ICR_TRIGGER_EDGE | (ICR_DELIVERY_STARTUP | (vector as u32)));
+    for _ in 0..100000 { core::hint::spin_loop(); }
+    // SIPI #2 (recommended)
+    send_ipi(apic_id, ICR_DEST_PHYSICAL | ICR_TRIGGER_EDGE | (ICR_DELIVERY_STARTUP | (vector as u32)));
+}

new file mode 100644
index 0000000..5c6a5cf
--- /dev/null
+++ b/src/arch/x86_64/smp.rs
@@ -0,0 +1,232 @@
+//! Minimal SMP bring-up for self-test: BSP starts one AP via INIT/SIPI/SIPI to a low 4K trampoline.
+//! Assumes APIC is enabled and LAPIC/IOAPIC mapped (feature "apic").
+//! For QEMU `-smp 2`, APIC IDs are typically {0,1}.
+
+use core::sync::atomic::{AtomicU32, AtomicU8, Ordering};
+use x86_64::{PhysAddr, VirtAddr};
+use crate::kernel::serial;
+use crate::arch::x86_64::{apic, memory};
+
+// Trampoline placement (physical): 0x8000 (vector 0x8). Must be identity-mapped and present.
+const AP_TRAMP_PHYS: u64 = 0x0000_8000;
+const AP_TRAMP_VECTOR: u8 = (AP_TRAMP_PHYS >> 12) as u8; // 4K page number
+
+// Shared online flags / counters indexed by slot (not strictly LAPIC ID; map below).
+static BSP_APIC_ID: AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0xFFFF_FFFF);
+static AP_APIC_ID:  AtomicU32 = AtomicU32::new(0xFFFF_FFFF);
+static CPU0_ONLINE:  AtomicU8  = AtomicU8::new(0);
+static CPU1_ONLINE:  AtomicU8  = AtomicU8::new(0);
+
+// Exported so the AP entry can signal "online".
+#[no_mangle]
+pub extern "C" fn smp_ap_online_report(apic_id: u32) {
+    if apic_id == BSP_APIC_ID.load(Ordering::SeqCst) {
+        CPU0_ONLINE.store(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
+    } else {
+        CPU1_ONLINE.store(1, Ordering::SeqCst);
+    }
+    serial::write_str("[smp] cpu=");
+    crate::kernel::serial::write_u64(apic_id as u64);
+    serial::write_str(" online\n");
+}
+
+/// Map trampoline page identity into the current address space and copy the embedded stub.
+unsafe fn deploy_trampoline() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
+    // Map the physical page identity at the same VA (simple for QEMU selftest).
+    // If your paging forbids low identity, you can pick a fixed VA and still SIPI to the phys.
+    memory::map_mmio_region(PhysAddr::new(AP_TRAMP_PHYS), 0x1000)
+        .map_err(|_| "map trampoline failed")?;
+    // Copy code bytes from our linked section into the physical page.
+    extern "C" {
+        static __ap_tramp_start: u8;
+        static __ap_tramp_end:   u8;
+    }
+    let src = &__ap_tramp_start as *const u8;
+    let end = &__ap_tramp_end as *const u8;
+    let len = end as usize - src as usize;
+    let dst = AP_TRAMP_PHYS as *mut u8;
+    for i in 0..len {
+        core::ptr::write_volatile(dst.add(i), core::ptr::read_volatile(src.add(i)));
+    }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// Bring up the second core in QEMU and start its LAPIC timer.
+pub fn init_smp_2() -> Result<(), &'static str> {
+    if !cfg!(feature = "apic") {
+        return Err("APIC required for SMP");
+    }
+    if !apic::lapic_base_is_mapped() {
+        return Err("LAPIC not initialized");
+    }
+    unsafe { deploy_trampoline()?; }
+
+    // Record BSP APIC ID.
+    let bsp_id = apic::lapic_id();
+    BSP_APIC_ID.store(bsp_id, Ordering::SeqCst);
+
+    // Pick a target APIC ID to wake. In QEMU -smp 2, it’s usually 1 if BSP is 0.
+    // If BSP is 1, try 0. (Best-effort heuristic for selftest.)
+    let target = if bsp_id == 0 { 1 } else { 0 };
+    AP_APIC_ID.store(target, Ordering::SeqCst);
+
+    serial::write_str("[smp] bsp apic=");
+    crate::kernel::serial::write_u64(bsp_id as u64);
+    serial::write_str(" target=");
+    crate::kernel::serial::write_u64(target as u64);
+    serial::write_str("\n");
+
+    unsafe { apic::start_ap(target, AP_TRAMP_VECTOR); }
+    Ok(())
+}
+
+/// Self-test: both CPUs run LAPIC timers; exit when each reaches 10 ticks (handled in ISR).
+#[cfg(all(feature = "idt-selftest", selftest_SMP_2))]
+pub fn selftest_all_online_and_ticks() -> bool {
+    use core::sync::atomic::Ordering;
+    if CPU0_ONLINE.load(Ordering::SeqCst) == 1 && CPU1_ONLINE.load(Ordering::SeqCst) == 1 {
+        // Tick thresholds are checked in scheduler’s LAPIC path; we just let the ISR signal exit.
+        true
+    } else {
+        false
+    }
+}

index 0000000..9b1b4b7
--- /dev/null
+++ b/src/arch/x86_64/smp_ap_trampoline.S
@@ -0,0 +1,129 @@
+// Minimal AP bootstrap: assumed SIPI to 0x8000 (vector 0x8).
+// Switch to protected mode → long mode, then call Rust ap_entry64().
+// NOTE: For self-test in QEMU, we assume BSP already set up page tables that include identity map
+// of low memory. For a production kernel, you’d build an AP-local minimal page table here.
+
+.code16
+.section .ap_tramp, "ax"
+.global __ap_tramp_start
+__ap_tramp_start:
+    cli
+    xor %ax, %ax
+    mov %ax, %ds
+    mov %ax, %es
+    mov %ax, %ss
+
+    // Enable A20
+    in   $0x92, %al
+    or   $0x02, %al
+    out  %al, $0x92
+
+    // Load temporary GDT (flat)
+    lgdt gdt_ptr
+
+    // CR0.PE=1 -> protected mode
+    mov %cr0, %eax
+    or  $0x1, %eax
+    mov %eax, %cr0
+
+    // Far jump to flush prefetch queue
+    ljmp $0x08, $prot32
+
+.code32
+prot32:
+    mov $0x10, %ax
+    mov %ax, %ds
+    mov %ax, %es
+    mov %ax, %ss
+
+    // Enable PAE
+    mov %cr4, %eax
+    or  $(1<<5), %eax     // PAE
+    mov %eax, %cr4
+
+    // Assume BSP page tables already installed; AP uses same CR3
+    // Enable long mode (EFER.LME)
+    mov $0xC0000080, %ecx
+    rdmsr
+    or  $(1<<8), %eax     // LME
+    wrmsr
+
+    // Paging on (CR0.PG=1)
+    mov %cr0, %eax
+    or  $(1<<31), %eax
+    mov %eax, %cr0
+
+    // Far jump to 64-bit mode
+    ljmp $0x08, $long64
+
+.code64
+long64:
+    // Call into Rust entry
+    mov $0, %rdi    // no args
+    call ap_entry64
+
+1:  hlt
+    jmp 1b
+
+// Simple flat GDT: null, code, data
+.align 8
+gdt:
+    .quad 0x0000000000000000
+    .quad 0x00AF9A000000FFFF    // code: base=0, limit=0xFFFFF, G=1, 64-bit
+    .quad 0x00AF92000000FFFF    // data: same
+gdt_end:
+gdt_ptr:
+    .word gdt_end - gdt - 1
+    .long gdt
+
+.global __ap_tramp_end
+__ap_tramp_end:
+
+.extern ap_entry64

+    }
     loop {
         arch::x86_64::cpu::halt();
     }

 //! Simple round-robin scheduler (skeleton).
 use crate::kernel::serial;

 #[cfg(all(feature = "idt-selftest", selftest_TIMER))]
 static mut TICK_COUNT: core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64 = core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64::new(0);
@@ -9,6 +10,11 @@ static mut LAPIC_TICK_COUNT: core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64 = core::sync::atomic
+#[cfg(all(feature="smp", feature="apic"))]
+static CPU_TICKS: [core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64; 2] = [
+    core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64::new(0),
+    core::sync::atomic::AtomicU64::new(0),
+];
 
 pub fn tick() {
     // Called from (PIT or LAPIC) timer ISR
     serial::write_str("⏳");
@@ -26,6 +32,27 @@ pub fn tick() {
         if (n % 10) == 0 {
             serial::write_str("[lapic-tick] n=10\n");
         }
+        #[cfg(feature="smp")]
+        {
+            use core::sync::atomic::Ordering;
+            let id = apic::lapic_id();
+            let idx = if id == 0 { 0 } else { 1 };
+            let ncpu = CPU_TICKS[idx].fetch_add(1, Ordering::SeqCst) + 1;
+            if (ncpu % 10) == 0 {
+                serial::write_str("[lapic-tick] cpu=");
+                crate::kernel::serial::write_u64(id as u64);
+                serial::write_str(" n=10\n");
+            }
+            // Selftest: exit when both CPUs reached 10 ticks.
+            #[cfg(all(feature = "idt-selftest", selftest_SMP_2))]
+            {
+                if CPU_TICKS[0].load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 10 &&
+                   CPU_TICKS[1].load(Ordering::SeqCst) >= 10 {
+                    unsafe { crate::arch::x86_64::io::qemu_exit(0x00); }
+                }
+            }
+        }
     }
 }
Notes

The AP trampoline is intentionally small and assumes your BSP already established page tables that include low identity (QEMU self-test). For a production path, you’d supply AP-local page tables via CR3 before enabling PG, or reuse the BSP tables explicitly.

We use a best-effort APIC ID heuristic (0→1 or 1→0) that works for QEMU -smp 2. For more CPUs, you’d enumerate MADT or MP tables.

Per-CPU tick logs: "[lapic-tick] cpu=<id> n=10" help the harness confirm both CPUs ticked.

Very feasible if you keep the kernel minimal and push heavy lifting to skill agents.

The hardest parts aren’t kernel tricks; they’re IOMMU/VFIO robustness on consumer GPUs, key/attestation lifecycle, and policy language that a human can maintain.

Your current kernel state is enough to anchor the control plane. You don’t need full POSIX—you need process model + IPC + capabilities + attestation next.

Suggested technical path
0–6 weeks: Master MVP (single box, two GPUs)
Kernel: add per-process address spaces, IPC, capability table; Ed25519 signing in userspace (or ring-3 crypto lib).

GPU isolation: one VFIO path stable (even headless); prove GPU pinning to Philosophy/Technical services.

Policy engine v1: TOML/YAML policy + “allow/deny with reason” + signed directives.

Wire protocol v1: QUIC + signed messages; idempotent commands; monotonic counters to prevent replay.

Two edge agents (Linux):

Jetson “vision-skill”

Pi “home-io-skill”

Demo: master approves requests, edges run work, artifacts return with provenance.

2–3 months: Reliability & orchestration
Work scheduler: simple queues with deadlines and budgets; GPU affinity respected.

Observability: structured logs, span IDs, per-node heartbeats; “quarantine” misbehaving edges.

Secrets: sealed keys per edge; short-lived capability tokens (macaroons/JWT-like with caveats).

Policy v2: composition (who/what/when/where), time windows, quorum approvals.

4–6 months: Product posture
IOMMU hardening on real hardware (Ryzen/Intel), recovery flows.

PF matrix & memory hardening in kernel; crash-only design for user services.

Versioned skill manifests; rolling updates; staged deployments; audit trails.

Hardware tiers (example builds)
Solo Dev (budget)

1× AMD 5600G APU (no dGPU), 32 GB RAM, NVMe

Edge: Raspberry Pi 4/5 + USB accelerators

Purpose: protocol/policy development, no heavy GPU.

Starter Master (you today)

Ryzen 5/7, 2× mid-range NVIDIA GPUs (e.g., RTX 4060/5060 class)

64 GB RAM, 1–2 TB NVMe

Edges: 1× Jetson Orin Nano (vision), 1× Pi 5 (GPIO)

Purpose: Philosophy/Technical pinned GPUs; 3–5 skills.

Prosumer Master

Ryzen 9, 2× RTX 4080/4090 mixed

128 GB RAM, 2–4 TB NVMe, 10GbE

Edges: 2–4 Jetsons, 2–3 x86 mini-PCs

Purpose: concurrent skills + heavier models; low-latency LAN.

Small Lab

Dual-socket Xeon/EPYC, 4× data-center GPUs (A10/A6000 used)

256 GB RAM, mirrored NVMe, 10GbE/25GbE

Edges: 10–20 nodes (Jetson + Pis + NUCs)

Purpose: multi-tenant skills, HA master, measurable SLOs.

Distributed Edge Fleet

Master as above, plus a backup master (warm standby)

50–200 edges; cellular/mesh links; key rotation infra

Purpose: real deployments with resilience.

Key design choices (keep it simple and safe)
Agents on Linux for now. Drivers are sane, CUDA/TensorRT works, GPIO easy. Your kernel stays lean.

One GPU per core (Philosophy/Technical). No MPS. Avoids contention and simplifies failure domains.

Capabilities everywhere: master issues capability tokens with explicit scope (resource, rate, time).

Message bus: point-to-point QUIC beats “fire-and-forget MQTT” when you need strong coupling and attestation. If you want pub/sub, run NATS/JetStream in user space on the master and put a capability gate in front.

Storage: append-only logs with hash chaining; artifacts stored on edges and pulled on demand (with proofs).

What can go wrong (so you plan for it)
VFIO pain on consumer GPUs: driver updates, quirks, resume/hibernate. Mitigate with pinned kernel + specific driver versions, scripted health checks, and a “fallback to non-passthrough” mode for dev.

Policy sprawl: unreadable policies become security holes. Mitigate with templates, tests, and human-readable diffs.

Edge drift: versions diverge. Mitigate with signed manifests, enforced minimum versions, and quarantine on mismatch.

Network jitter: QUIC helps, but design timeouts/retries/backoff carefully with idempotent operations.

How the 10 personal projects fit
Every one of those projects becomes a skill on an edge (or a few) with a thin capability contract, while the master owns policy/approval and final audit.
Examples:

Finance Guardian → x86 mini-PC skill (bank APIs), rate-limited and vendor-scoped

Smart Home Router → Pi skill (cams/locks), policies checked centrally

Research Pipeline → Jetson/PC skill (scrape/summarize with GPU), provenance tracked

Home Lab Cost Governor → cloud skill (FinOps), budgets enforced centrally

Concrete next steps
Kernel: process model + IPC + per-task page tables + capability table (minimal, not POSIX).

Master services (userspace):

Policy engine v1 (TOML + tests)

Key/attestation authority

Work scheduler with budgets & affinity

Edge agent (Rust on Linux): QUIC transport, capability tokens, health pings, command executor.

DevOps: one-click bring-up scripts for master + edge; golden-string tests you already love.

My verdict: This is a coherent, realistic long-term project. You’ve crossed the line from kernel tinkering to a credible governance OS appliance. Keep the kernel small, push skills to edges, double down on capabilities, attestation, and policy tests. You’ll end up with a central brain that actually orchestrates useful, safe automation across your life and projects—without collapsing under its own weight.

@@ -0,0 +1,132 @@
+//! Page-Fault Matrix selftests (v1).
+//! This module triggers specific user-mode faults without needing mapping helpers.
+//! We use Ring-3 transitions and deliberately touch VAs to cause PF with known EC bits.
+//!
+//! Cases in v1:
+//!  - NP_U_R  : user READ from unmapped VA         => P=0, U=1, W=0
+//!  - NP_U_W  : user WRITE to unmapped VA          => P=0, U=1, W=1
+//!  - US_VIOL : user READ from kernel VA (present) => P=1, U=1, W=0 (US violation)
+
+use crate::kernel::serial;
+use crate::arch::x86_64::io::qemu_exit;
+use core::arch::asm;
+
+// Chosen canonical addresses:
+// - Unmapped user VA:   0x0000_7FFF_F000_0000 (typical empty region in our tests)
+// - Kernel VA (present): 0xFFFF_8000_0000_0000 (higher half, present in your kernel)
+const TEST_UNMAPPED_USER_VA: u64 = 0x0000_7FFF_F000_0000;
+const TEST_KERNEL_VA:        u64 = 0xFFFF_8000_0000_0000;
+
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn ring3_trigger_read(ptr: u64) -> ! {
+    // Execute in Ring-3: load from [ptr] to cause a fault in user mode.
+    // We reuse your Ring-3 trampoline infra: move RAX (service) and RBX (argument),
+    // then int 0x80 to enter the syscall handler that immediately iret back
+    // to this user-mode snippet encoded here.
+    //
+    // Instead of cross-calling, we directly craft a tiny user-mode stub below via inline asm.
+    //
+    // User snippet:
+    //   mov rdi, [rbx]   ; read from ptr -> PF
+    //   ud2              ; should never reach
+    //
+    // We jump to Ring-3 via your existing mechanism: set up iret frame elsewhere
+    // (already implemented in your Ring-3 selftest). For simplicity here we rely
+    // on a unified entry that runs a provided user thunk. If you don’t have it,
+    // call this from your existing RING3 test wrapper that does the iret dance.
+    asm!(
+        "mov rbx, {ptr}",
+        // switch to user via int 0x80 service  (service id loaded in rax)
+        // In your handler, detect this service and iret to a user stub.
+        "mov rax, 0x4000_0001",       // service tag: run_user_read
+        "int 0x80",
+        ptr = in(reg) ptr,
+        options(noreturn)
+    )
+}
+
+#[inline(always)]
+unsafe fn ring3_trigger_write(ptr: u64) -> ! {
+    // User snippet:
+    //   mov qword ptr [rbx], 1  ; write -> PF
+    //   ud2
+    asm!(
+        "mov rbx, {ptr}",
+        "mov rax, 0x4000_0002",       // service tag: run_user_write
+        "int 0x80",
+        ptr = in(reg) ptr,
+        options(noreturn)
+    )
+}
+
+#[inline(always)]
+pub fn start(case: &str) {
+    serial::write_str("[selftest] PFM: ");
+    serial::write_str(case);
+    serial::write_str("\n");
+    unsafe {
+        match case {
+            "NP_U_R"  => ring3_trigger_read(TEST_UNMAPPED_USER_VA),
+            "NP_U_W"  => ring3_trigger_write(TEST_UNMAPPED_USER_VA),
+            "US_VIOL" => ring3_trigger_read(TEST_KERNEL_VA),
+            _ => {
+                serial::write_str("[pf] unknown case\n");
+                qemu_exit(0x01);
+            }
+        }
+    }
+}
+
+/// Called by the page-fault handler in selftest mode once it decodes the error code.
+/// If the decoded bits match the expected case, exit success.
+pub fn verify_and_exit(case: &str, present: bool, user: bool, write: bool, instr_fetch: bool) {
+    use crate::arch::x86_64::io::qemu_exit;
+    let (want_p, want_u, want_w, want_id) = match case {
+        "NP_U_R"  => (false, true,  false, false),
+        "NP_U_W"  => (false, true,  true,  false),
+        "US_VIOL" => (true,  true,  false, false), // present, but U/S violation when user touched kernel VA
+        _ => {
+            serial::write_str("[pf] verify: unknown case\n");
+            unsafe { qemu_exit(0x02); }
+            return;
+        }
+    };
+    let ok = (present == want_p) && (user == want_u) && (write == want_w) && (instr_fetch == want_id);
+    if ok {
+        serial::write_str("[pf] case=");
+        serial::write_str(case);
+        serial::write_str(" ok\n");
+        unsafe { qemu_exit(0x00); }
+    } else {
+        serial::write_str("[pf] case=");
+        serial::write_str(case);
+        serial::write_str(" mismatch\n");
+        unsafe { qemu_exit(0x03); }
+    }
+}

+

+    serial::write_str(" ec=");
+    if present { serial::write_str("P=1 "); } else { serial::write_str("P=0 "); }
+    if user    { serial::write_str("U=1 "); } else { serial::write_str("U=0 "); }
+    if write   { serial::write_str("W=1 "); } else { serial::write_str("W=0 "); }
+    if instr_fetch { serial::write_str("ID=1"); } else { serial::write_str("ID=0"); }
+    serial::write_str("\n");
+
+    // Selftest path: determine which case we’re running (via cfg)
+    #[cfg(feature="pf-matrix")]
+    {
+        let case =
+            if cfg!(selftest_PFM_NP_U_R)  { "NP_U_R" }
+            else if cfg!(selftest_PFM_NP_U_W) { "NP_U_W" }
+            else if cfg!(selftest_PFM_US_VIOL){ "US_VIOL" }
+            else { "" };
+
+        if !case.is_empty() {
+            pf_matrix::verify_and_exit(case, present, user, write, instr_fetch);
+            // no return
+        }
+    }
 
     // Production behavior: log and halt (unchanged)
     loop { crate::arch::x86_64::cpu::halt(); }
 }
 
+// Hook point: in your main init, after IDT is loaded and Ring-3 infra is ready,
+// call pf_matrix::start("CASE") when the corresponding selftest cfg is set.
+
+diff --git a/qemu.sh b/qemu.sh
+index 7a5f2f2..f21f31b 100755

+++ b/qemu.sh
@@ -62,6 +62,30 @@ case "${TEST}" in
     FEATURES="idt-selftest,apic,smp"
     RUSTCFG="--cfg selftest_SMP_2"
